title: Mercy to captives
hookLine: the prisoners of Badr are fed well, and some freed for teaching Muslim children to read

lines: THE MEN WHO DROVE THEM OUT.
cards: The battle is over, and the Muslims of Medina have something they've never had before: about seventy prisoners. Men from Mecca, some of whom had mocked them, boycotted them, driven them from their homes.
Some are relatives: cousins, brothers, an uncle. In that world, a captive's life was in his captor's hands.

The prisoners are marched back to Medina, tied up, and divided among Muslim households, to be held until their families can pay a ransom. What would you expect? What happened next surprised even the prisoners.

teach.h: THEY GAVE THE ENEMY THE BREAD.
teach.b: The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told his companions to treat the captives well. The early biographer Ibn Ishaq keeps the memory of one prisoner, Abu 'Aziz, who described it afterward.

The Ansar family holding him gave him the bread, the better food, and ate only dates themselves, because of what the Prophet had told them. He'd hand the bread back, embarrassed, and they'd give it right back to him.
Food was not plentiful in Medina. They gave the enemy the good part.

teach.h: FOR THE LOVE OF GOD, NO THANKS.
teach.b: The Qur'an praises this kind of thing elsewhere: the righteous feed the needy, the orphan and the prisoner, for the love of God, wanting no reward and no thanks. Then the ransom. Families in Mecca paid to free their men.
But some prisoners were poor, with no one to pay.

A report from Ibn 'Abbas, in the Musnad of Ahmad, says the Prophet set a different price for some of them: teach the children of the Ansar to write, and you're free. Later tellings say ten children each.
A young community, fighting for its life, and what it asks of its enemies is literacy for its kids.
Tradition says one of the children who learned this way was Zayd ibn Thabit, later one of the main scribes of the Qur'an.
One more detail: the Prophet's own uncle, al-'Abbas, was among the captives. Ibn Sa'd says the Prophet couldn't sleep that night, hearing him groan in his ropes, until they were loosened.

how: Muslims often cite the captives of Badr and Qur'an 76:8 when teaching about the humane treatment of prisoners, and the ransom of literacy is remembered as an early honoring of learning.

games.q: a prisoner from Mecca can't pay a ransom. no one at home will pay for him. what does the Prophet ask of him?
o: work in the date groves for a year.
teach children of the Ansar to write.
stay a prisoner until someone pays.
games.why: teach the children to write, and go free. a community fighting to survive asked its enemies for literacy.

practice: Think of one thing you know how to do that someone near you doesn't: a dish, changing a tire, a phrase in another language, a shortcut on the computer, how to make wudu if that's yours to teach.
Picture the person, and the moment you'd show them, patiently, the way the prisoners of Badr taught children to shape their letters.

wordCard.voice: Mercy to captives. After Badr, prisoners were fed with the better food, and some were freed for teaching Muslim children to read and write. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a captive, a prisoner. the word used in 76:8.

carryVoice: Your line: freedom for teaching. Bread first, then letters for the children. I'll see you tomorrow.
